questions.question: Why is $\varnothing\subseteq A$ true for every set $A$?
options: Because there is no element of $\varnothing$ that could fail to belong to $A$
Because every set must contain $\varnothing$ as an element, in every case without exception.
Because $A$ must have at least one element
Because $\varnothing$ and $A$ have the same elements
questions.explanation: The empty set is a subset of every set A because there is no element of the empty set that could fail to belong to A.
questions.source_support: The empty set has no elements, so the subset condition has no counterexample.
questions.rewrite_notes: stem-option-quality auto: removed generator_residue/source_dependent_scaffolding; rebalanced distractor length to prevent answer leak.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: This confuses subset with membership: $\varnothing\subseteq A$ means every element of $\varnothing$ lies in $A$ (vacuously true), whereas $\varnothing\in A$ means $A$ lists $\varnothing$ as an element. For $A=\{1\}$, $\varnothing\subseteq\{1\}$ holds but $\varnothing\notin\{1\}$.

$\varnothing\subseteq A$ holds even for $A=\varnothing$: every set is a subset of itself, so $\varnothing\subseteq\varnothing$ is true, yet $\varnothing$ has no elements. Having at least one element is not required because the subset condition is vacuous.

Having the same elements would mean $\varnothing=A$, but $\varnothing\subseteq A$ holds for every $A$, including $A=\{1\}$ where $\varnothing\ne\{1\}$; the reason is vacuous truth, not equality of elements.
